# Exactly tractable circuits and space–time duality {#sec-exact-circuits}

Exact solutions are often associated with noninteracting or integrable systems.
Dual-unitary circuits reveal another possibility: a dynamics can be strongly
entangling and nonintegrable while selected many-body observables remain exactly
calculable. Their special structure concerns how a tensor network can be
contracted, rather than an extensive set of conventional conserved charges.

We develop the mechanism using only finite-dimensional linear algebra, partial
traces, and elementary entanglement. Use $\hbar=k_B=1$, natural logarithms, and
local Hilbert-space dimension $d$. For qubits, $\sigma^a$ are Pauli matrices and
$S^a=\sigma^a/2$. Gate rotation angles below multiply Pauli matrices explicitly;
they should not be interpreted as the same numerical coupling multiplying $S^a$.

## A gate with two interpretations

A two-site unitary has matrix elements
$U_{ab}^{cd}=\langle c,d|U|a,b\rangle$, where each index takes $d$ values.
Ordinary unitarity is

$$
\sum_{cd}U_{ab}^{cd}(U_{a'b'}^{cd})^*
=\delta_{aa'}\delta_{bb'}.
$$ {#eq-dual-time-unitarity}

In a circuit drawn vertically in time, this identity cancels a gate with its
adjoint when their outgoing legs are contracted.
Now regroup the same four indices into a different matrix:

$$
\widetilde U_{ac}^{bd}=U_{ab}^{cd}.
$$ {#eq-dual-reshuffle}

This *reshuffling* changes which pair of legs is treated as input. A gate is
**dual unitary** when $\widetilde U$ is also unitary:

$$
\sum_{bd}U_{ab}^{cd}(U_{a'b}^{c'd})^*
=\delta_{aa'}\delta_{cc'}.
$$ {#eq-dual-space-unitarity}

The second equation permits a cancellation in the spatial direction. It is not
true for a generic unitary gate. Reshuffling is also not the usual partial
transpose, despite involving a related regrouping of indices. Specify the index
map when implementing either operation.

Arrange copies of $U$ in alternating layers of nearest-neighbor gates, a
*brickwork circuit*. Temporal unitarity preserves norm under physical time
evolution. Dual unitarity permits certain tensor-network contractions to be
performed sideways. Space is not literally a second physical time; a different
linear-algebra contraction happens to be unitary.

## Constructing and checking an explicit family

The SWAP gate acts as $W|a,b\rangle=|b,a\rangle$ and has
$W_{ab}^{cd}=\delta_{cb}\delta_{da}$. Its reshuffling is another permutation
matrix, so it is dual unitary. SWAP alone is not chaotic: it merely transports
local states.

A more instructive family is

$$
U_\phi|a,b\rangle=e^{i\phi_{ab}}|b,a\rangle.
$$ {#eq-dual-phase-swap}

For each input pair there is one output pair of modulus-one amplitude, proving
ordinary unitarity. For each reshuffled row $(a,c)$, the only allowed column is
$(b,d)=(c,a)$, again with modulus one. This proves dual unitarity for arbitrary
real phases $\phi_{ab}$.
For qubits, $U=\mathrm{SWAP}\,e^{-i\gamma\sigma^z\otimes\sigma^z}$ is an
example. It entangles generic product states, yet its diagonal spin operators
follow simple trajectories. Entangling power and chaos are different criteria.

Multiplying by arbitrary single-site unitaries on incoming and outgoing legs
preserves both cancellation identities:
$U'=(u_1\otimes u_2)U(v_1\otimes v_2)$.
Suitable choices produce much richer dynamics. Some dual-unitary gates are
mixing, some have persistent local modes, and some belong to integrable families.
Dual unitarity alone does not select one of these behaviors.

The following Julia calculation verifies the index convention explicitly rather
than relying on an ambiguous multidimensional reshape:

```julia
#| eval: false
using LinearAlgebra
d = 2
ix(a,b) = a*d+b+1  # a,b start at zero
U = zeros(ComplexF64,d^2,d^2)
gamma = 0.37
for a in 0:d-1, b in 0:d-1
    phase = exp(-im*gamma*(1-2a)*(1-2b))
    U[ix(b,a),ix(a,b)] = phase
end
R = similar(U)
for a in 0:d-1, b in 0:d-1, c in 0:d-1, e in 0:d-1
    R[ix(a,c),ix(b,e)] = U[ix(c,e),ix(a,b)]
end
@assert norm(U' * U - I) < 1e-12
@assert norm(R' * R - I) < 1e-12
```

A useful negative control is a generic two-qubit unitary: it passes the first
assertion and almost always fails the second. This protects against a code path
that accidentally checks ordinary unitarity twice.

## Deriving the light-ray correlation channel

Consider the infinite-temperature correlator of traceless local observables,

$$
C_{ab}(x,t)=d^{-L}\operatorname{Tr}
\left[U(t)^\dagger a_0U(t)b_x\right].
$$ {#eq-dual-correlator}

The trace is a network with a forward circuit, a backward circuit, and two
operator insertions. Outside the causal cone, ordinary unitarity cancels the
two layers. Inside the cone, dual unitarity cancels transverse pairs. If a
traceless insertion is left disconnected from the other insertion, the network
vanishes because $\operatorname{tr}a=0$.
For one-site observables in a homogeneous dual-unitary brickwork circuit, the
remaining nonzero contributions lie on the appropriate maximal-velocity rays,
with checkerboard parity deciding which edge is accessible for a given
insertion. This is an exact infinite-temperature statement, not a generic
property of thermal correlation functions.

Along a right-moving ray, a single edge gate induces the map

$$
\mathcal M_R(a)=\frac1d\operatorname{tr}_1
\left[U^\dagger(a\otimes\mathbf1)U\right].
$$ {#eq-dual-channel}

The trace removes the first site; the output is an operator on the second.
A left-moving map is defined with the two sites interchanged. Each map is a
completely positive, trace-preserving, unital channel: it comes from unitary
conjugation with a maximally mixed environment. A normalized correlation after
$n$ successive equivalent edge gates reduces to

$$
C_{ab}^{R}(n)=\frac1d\operatorname{tr}
\left[\mathcal M_R^{\,n}(a)b\right].
$$ {#eq-dual-channel-power}

If gates alternate within a unit cell, the corresponding channel composition
replaces the simple power. Reporting $n$ as the number of edge gates avoids
confusing a single brickwork layer with a full two-layer Floquet period.
The exact reduction is the central result behind @bertini2019dual.

Diagonalize $\mathcal M_R$ in the $d^2$-dimensional single-site operator space.
The identity has eigenvalue one. A traceless eigenoperator $r$ with eigenvalue
$\lambda$ contributes $\lambda^n$ to a ray correlation. Eigenvalues inside the
unit circle give exponential decay along that ray; unit-modulus eigenvalues
produce persistent or oscillatory pieces. Jordan blocks can add polynomial
prefactors. A channel gap concerns these local ray observables; it does not
by itself prove every possible many-body notion of ergodicity.

## Worked example: a nonmixing dual-unitary gate

For the phased SWAP with qubit angle $\gamma$,
$U^\dagger(\sigma^z\otimes\mathbf1)U=\mathbf1\otimes\sigma^z$.
Thus $\mathcal M_R(\sigma^z)=\sigma^z$: magnetization travels without decay.
For $\sigma^x$, conjugation by the controlled phase produces terms proportional
to $\mathbf1\otimes\sigma^x$ and $\sigma^z\otimes\sigma^y$.
The partial trace removes the second term and gives

$$
\mathcal M_R(\sigma^x)=\cos(2\gamma)\sigma^x,
\qquad
\mathcal M_R(\sigma^y)=\cos(2\gamma)\sigma^y.
$$ {#eq-dual-example-channel}

The $x$ and $y$ ray correlations decay geometrically for generic $\gamma$,
while the $z$ correlation does not. The same gate can therefore be mixing in
some observable sectors and exactly nonmixing in another. This is a concrete
reason to examine the full traceless channel spectrum rather than infer chaos
from one rapidly decaying correlation.

Interior two-point functions can vanish even though the state is highly
entangled. Information may reside in operators supported on many sites.
Out-of-time-ordered correlators use four rather than two circuit replicas and
probe a different contraction problem. Dual unitarity simplifies many of them,
but one must establish the relevant replica identities rather than assume every
higher moment follows from @eq-dual-channel-power.

## Entanglement: the cut bound and exact saturation

Represent a pure-state circuit as a tensor network with local legs of dimension
$d$. Draw a cut through the network separating final region $A$ from its
complement. If it crosses $r$ legs, the Schmidt rank is at most $d^r$.
For every Rényi entropy with positive index, the entropy is bounded by the
logarithm of rank:

$$
S_A^{(n)}\leq r\ln d.
$$ {#eq-dual-cut-bound}

Minimize over allowed cuts to obtain the strongest such bound. The logic needs
only the factorization of the network across cut indices. It is a bound, not
an equality for a generic circuit or initial state.

For certain solvable initial product or short-range entangled states in
self-dual kicked Ising and related dual-unitary circuits, repeated cancellations
show that the nonzero eigenvalues of the reduced state are all equal. If the
rank is $d^r$, then

$$
\rho_A\;\text{has spectrum}\;
\underbrace{d^{-r},\ldots,d^{-r}}_{d^r\ \mathrm{entries}},
\qquad S_A^{(n)}=r\ln d.
$$ {#eq-dual-flat-spectrum}

Indeed, $\operatorname{tr}\rho_A^n=d^{-r(n-1)}$, which directly yields the
same entropy for every Rényi index and the von Neumann limit. This proves
minimal-cut saturation for those states, rather than guessing it from a large
entanglement velocity. For a long interval and suitable circuit units the
leading result has the familiar form
$S_\ell(t)=\min(2t,\ell)\ln d$, with boundary/parity offsets determined by
the precise layer and initial-state convention.

@bertini2019entanglement constructs this exact solvable class. Arbitrary
product states need not share every finite-time equality. Generic chaotic
systems are instead described at large scales by a membrane with a nontrivial
line tension [@zhou2020membrane]. A cut bound, exact flat spectrum, and a
coarse-grained membrane are three related but logically different statements.

## Exact spectral correlations: another notion of chaos

Local relaxation does not exhaust quantum chaos diagnostics. For a Floquet
operator $U_F$ with eigenphases $\theta_j$, define the spectral form factor

$$
K(t)=\left\langle|\operatorname{Tr}U_F^t|^2\right\rangle
=\left\langle\sum_{jk}e^{it(\theta_j-\theta_k)}\right\rangle.
$$ {#eq-dual-sff}

The brackets specify an ensemble or smoothing procedure. Random-matrix
predictions depend on antiunitary symmetries: the early ramp is proportional to
$t$ for the circular unitary ensemble and approximately $2t$ for the circular
orthogonal ensemble at times small compared with Hilbert-space dimension.
One must resolve exact symmetries before making the comparison.

For the kicked Ising chain,

$$
U_F=e^{-ib\sum_x\sigma_x^x}
\exp\!\left[-i\left(J\sum_x\sigma_x^z\sigma_{x+1}^z+
\sum_xh_x\sigma_x^z\right)\right],
$$ {#eq-dual-kicked-ising}

self-dual angles satisfy $|J|=|b|=\pi/4$. After a suitable longitudinal-field
ensemble average, the folded space–time network reduces the form factor to a
transfer problem whose dominant states can be identified. @bertini2018spectral
establishes random-matrix form-factor behavior in the thermodynamic limit at
fixed time for this setting. The original paper proves the odd-time result
rigorously and presents a precise conjecture for even times. That historical
qualification should be retained when describing what that paper established.

The order of limits matters: a fixed-time, infinite-length result is not a
uniform theorem up to the exponentially large Heisenberg time for one finite
sample. A field ensemble average is also not identical to every individual
realization. Exact solvability makes assumptions easier to inspect; it does
not eliminate them.

## The gate as a four-party quantum state

Dual unitarity also has a direct information-theoretic meaning. Convert a gate
into its normalized *Choi state* by attaching maximally entangled references to
its two inputs:

$$
|U\rangle=\frac1d\sum_{abcd}U_{ab}^{cd}|a\rangle_A|b\rangle_B
|c\rangle_C|d\rangle_D.
$$ {#eq-dual-choi}

The labels $A,B$ represent input reference indices and $C,D$ output indices.
Ordinary unitarity ensures normalization and makes the reduced state on $AB$
equal to $\mathbf1_{AB}/d^2$. Every unitary is therefore maximally entangled
across the input/output partition $AB|CD$ in this state representation.

Now examine the crossed partition $AC|BD$. Its coefficient matrix is
$\widetilde U/d$, so

$$
\rho_{AC}=\frac{\widetilde U\widetilde U^\dagger}{d^2}.
$$ {#eq-dual-choi-reduction}

Dual unitarity is exactly the statement that this reduced state is also
$\mathbf1_{AC}/d^2$. The gate has maximal operator entanglement across that
crossed partition. The extra cancellation identity and this entropy statement
are two ways of describing the same algebraic constraint.

There is still a third two-two partition, $AD|BC$. Dual unitarity does not force
it to be maximally entangled. For SWAP, the Choi state factorizes into maximally
entangled pairs linking $A$ with $D$ and $B$ with $C$; it is a product across
$AD|BC$. A four-party tensor that is maximally entangled across every balanced
partition is a stronger object, often called a perfect tensor in this setting.
A dual-unitary gate should not automatically be called perfect.

This example separates three uses of entanglement. Operator entanglement is
entanglement of a map represented as a state. State entanglement is generated
when that map acts on a specified input. Scrambling concerns how local input
information becomes encoded across many output degrees of freedom. Maximal
operator entanglement in two partitions does not imply every input is maximally
entangled or every observable is mixing. The phased-SWAP example already gives
a counterexample to such an inference.

![The phased-SWAP ray channel at $\gamma=0.37$. Julia matrix iteration agrees
with the exact $X$ eigenvalue $\cos(2\gamma)$ while the $Z$ mode persists.
This dual-unitary example intentionally retains a nonmixing sector.](figs/dual-channel.png){#fig-dual-channel width=80%}

The numerical check in [numerics/transport_labs.jl](numerics/transport_labs.jl)
constructs both the ordinary and reshuffled gate and evaluates the partial trace
channel directly. It compares the entire known eigenmode trajectory, rather
than fitting an exponential decay rate to a few points. This makes the example
a useful unit test for conventions before studying a more complicated
space–time-dual model.

## How to use exact circuits as research laboratories

A useful reproduction ladder is: verify the reshuffled gate numerically;
construct its one-site channels; predict ray correlators from channel powers;
compare to explicit small-chain evolution; then explore an initial-state class
for entanglement or an ensemble for the form factor. Each step has an analytic
answer and an independent implementation.

Next perturb away from dual unitarity. The formerly perfect cancellations fail,
allowing one to study how interior correlations, front broadening, and generic
membrane behavior emerge. Small deviations need not be uniformly small at long
time because the number of imperfect contractions grows. Establishing a
controlled expansion and its breakdown scale is itself a research problem.

The 2026 review @bertini2026duality surveys the broad space–time-duality program,
including exactly tractable yet chaotic dynamics. It provides a route from the
simple identities derived here to more sophisticated replica and transfer-matrix
methods. The central conceptual lesson is operational: “solvable” refers to a
specified observable and contraction, while “chaotic” refers to a specified
dynamical or spectral diagnostic.

## Exercises and selected solutions

1. Prove dual unitarity of @eq-dual-phase-swap directly from both index identities.
   Give an example of phases that entangle a product state.
2. Show that local unitary dressings preserve dual unitarity. Identify the
   corresponding unitary transformations on the reshuffled matrix's legs.
3. Derive the three traceless eigenvalues of the phased-SWAP ray channel. Compare
   them with exact two-qubit correlations for one gate.
4. Prove the Schmidt-rank bound for a network cut and derive all Rényi entropies
   of a flat reduced-state spectrum.
5. Compute $K(t)$ for small kicked Ising chains after resolving symmetries.
   Compare a field ensemble average with individual samples and report variance.
6. Perturb a dual-unitary gate by a small generic two-qubit unitary. Quantify the
   dual-unitarity defect and test how the ray-channel prediction fails with time.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution: an entangling phased SWAP"}
Apply $e^{-i\gamma\sigma^z\otimes\sigma^z}$ to $|+,+\rangle$.
The one-qubit reduced state has eigenvalues
$[1\pm|\cos2\gamma|]/2$. SWAP does not change them. At $\gamma=\pi/4$,
they are both $1/2$, so the output is maximally entangled. Yet
$\mathcal M_R(\sigma^z)=\sigma^z$ still holds. Maximal entanglement of this
input does not imply mixing of all local observables.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution sketch: a cut is a rank factorization"}
Collect the cut indices into one label $\alpha$ with at most $d^r$ values.
The wavefunction factorizes as
$\psi_{ij}=\sum_\alpha L_{i\alpha}R_{\alpha j}$, so its matrix rank is at most
$d^r$. The Schmidt rank equals that matrix rank. Among density matrices of
rank at most $d^r$, the uniform spectrum maximizes every positive-index Rényi
entropy. This yields @eq-dual-cut-bound and states exactly what must be shown
to claim saturation.
:::
